The Atacama Desert. The driest non-polar desert on Earth, stretching roughly six hundred miles along the western edge of the Andes in Chile, Peru, and Bolivia. Some meteorological stations in its core have recorded no measurable rainfall in recorded history, making it an extreme environment where virtually no vegetation exists outside of rare oases.

Located on South America's Pacific coast, wedged between the Andes Mountains to the east and the cold Pacific to the west, the Atacama presents one of Earth's harshest landscapes. Some portions have not experienced rainfall for over four hundred years. Parts of the Atacama Pampa are so dry that human mummies naturally preserve without any intervention.

The Humboldt Current, a cold ocean current, prevents moisture-laden clouds from crossing inland, creating a permanent rain shadow that keeps the interior bone-dry. Rich in mineral deposits, including copper, nitrates historically extracted for explosives and fertilizer, and lithium, the Atacama is economically vital to Chile.

The desert contains the Valle de la Luna, the Valley of the Moon, a striking landscape of colorful rock formations shaped by wind erosion over millennia. Indigenous Atacameño peoples adapted to the desert using underground water sources and cultivating hardy crops in scattered oases. The extreme dryness and thin atmosphere make it ideal for astronomical observation. Major observatories are located here to take advantage of these conditions.

The Atacama's extreme climate creates an environment shaped by the Andes Mountains to its east and the cold Humboldt Current to its west, demonstrating how orographic and oceanic forces create one of Earth's most inhospitable regions. Its abundance of copper and other minerals, combined with its scientific importance for astronomy, underscore the Atacama's significance despite its aridity.
